claim: US average device age at trade-in/upgrade (Assurant data) rose from 3.16 years in 2020 to 3.84 years in the first three quarters of 2025, an increase of 0.68 years (about 8 months) over 5 years.
stance_target: structural, multi-year lengthening of the replacement cycle
scope_conditions: US, Assurant Mobile Trade-in and Upgrade Industry Trends reports, 2020-2025
quoted_support: Assurant's Mobile Trade-in and Upgrade Industry Trends report tells us that in 2020 the average age of devices traded-in or upgraded (the replacement lifecycle) was 3.16 years... Data for the first three quarters of 2025 show that the average lifecycle is 3.84 years so far in 2025. That's an increase of 0.68 years or just over 8 months in 5 years.

claim: iPhone-specific average trade-in/upgrade age rose from 3.27 years (2020) to 3.67 years (2024), a smaller increase (+0.40yr) than Android's rise from 2.79 to 3.52 years (+0.73yr), narrowing the iPhone-Android gap to 0.15 years by 2024.
stance_target: iPhone-specific replacement cycle trend and its convergence with Android
quoted_support: iPhone has gone from 3.27 years in 2020, to 3.67 years in 2024. That's an increase of 0.4 years... Android has gone from 2.79 years in 2020 to 3.52 years in 2024 which is a much sharper increase of 0.73 years... the difference is just 0.15 years.

claim: Global smartphone replacement cycle rose from a 2013 low of 2.4 years to a 2022 peak of 3.7 years, easing to 3.5 years in 2024-2025.
stance_target: global (not just US) structural lengthening of replacement cycle, with a plateau/slight reversal post-2022 peak
scope_conditions: global, unattributed composite series (source not explicitly named in article)
quoted_support: in 2013, consumer smartphones had an average replacement cycle length of 2.4 years... by 2022, the global figure for smartphone upgrades had reached its highest since 2013. The upgrade cycle reached 3.7 years... average lifecycle of a smartphone in 2025 is 3.5 years.

claim: Reasons consumers give for upgrading their smartphone (Counterpoint Research survey): battery performance 75%, screen damage 55%, keeping up to date 38%, device no longer works 38%, price/value 30%, image quality 24%, prettier phone 17%, too slow 13%, app compatibility 5% -- AI/AI features are not listed as a stated upgrade driver.
stance_target: AI features are a primary driver of upgrade decisions
scope_conditions: Counterpoint Research consumer survey, cited via SellCell
quoted_support: Battery performance 75%, Screen damage 55%, Keeping up to date 38%, No longer works 38%, Price / Value (switching-related, US) 30%, Image quality 24%, Prettier smartphone 17%, Too slow 13%, App compatibility 5%.

claim: CIRP data shows iPhone owners keep devices longer than Android owners: 61% of iPhone owners keep their phone 2-3 years and 29% keep it 3+ years, versus 43% and 21% respectively for Android owners.
stance_target: iPhone-specific replacement cycle lengthening and Apple's stronger device longevity/loyalty profile
quoted_support: 61.0% of Apple owners keep their phone for between two to three years, compared to 43.0% of Android owners. 29.0% of iPhone owners make it over three years with their handset. Only 21.0% of people with Android owners manage this.

claim: SellCell's 2026 Smartphone Loyalty Survey found 83.8% of iPhone users have stayed with Apple more than five years, versus 33.8% of Android users, and that brand-switching intent falls sharply the longer a device is held (23.1% of Android users upgrading within 6 months say they'd switch brands vs 9.4% of those waiting 2+ years).
stance_target: lengthening replacement cycles correlate with entrenched loyalty/retention rather than churn risk, favorable for Apple's installed-base durability
quoted_support: It found that 83.8% of iPhone users have stayed with Apple for more than five years, compared with 33.8% of Android users... Among Android users planning to upgrade within the next six months, 23.1% said they would switch brands. For those waiting more than two years, that figure falls to 9.4%.
